c: I'm Rosie, the Managing Director of Eleos, which is a nonprofit researching potential

empirically. So why study AI welfare? Well, the

in the near future. And by moral consideration, we
mean something like it matters in its own right.
And this kind of means roughly the same as is a moral patient
or has moral status, and I'll introduce these relatively interchangeably during this talk.
But I'm not going to spend this talk
making the case for AI consciousness or AI welfare,
or going into depth about different definitions. What I'm more going to
focus on is if you take it seriously,
then here's a way you can approach it,
because I think a lot of people often think that it's just completely intractable.
So in this talk, I'll start with some
recent developments in AI welfare. I'll tell you a
little bit about Eleos, and then the bulk of
the talk will be on how we approach it.
So looking at targets of investigation, different types of evidence you can use,
prioritization criteria, and some interesting research directions.
All right. So, starting with some recent developments.
2025 was a big year for AI
welfare. There was a lot of industry activity.
Anthropic launched a formal AI welfare program and
did evaluations as part of the Claude 4
system card. They also trialed different interventions
such as letting Claude exit conversations, and they published a new constitution that
has a section on Claude's nature and well-being. Google also did some work on
this. They published some AI welfare research and
hosted a workshop. And OpenAI revised how
ChatGPT talks about consciousness and announced plans to study perceptions of consciousness.

we saw a significant increase in users who,
warranted or not, were perceiving AI systems
as conscious. And some of the more extreme cases of
this became known as AI psychosis. We saw the
start of some potentially concerning political backlash. Ohio and Missouri both introduced AI

coverage in lots of major outlets like the

the first Eleos conference on AI consciousness and welfare, where we brought together
around 200 experts across machine learning, philosophy, cognitive science, neuroscience,
and policy, all to get together and try
and make some progress on these issues.
So what are we actually trying to do here? What's the problem? Well,
AI is advancing faster than our understanding of consciousness and moral patienthood.
We are not ready, but we're already in a place
where we're having to discuss these issues and try
and figure out how to take some action.

answers anytime soon to a lot of these questions.

correspond to the truth of the matter about whether something is conscious. And so,

be better calibrated to avoid risks in both directions.

And broadly, we are trying to first identify a target of investigation,
secondly, to try and make use of different
types of evidence, and then finally, to select promising
directions using some prioritization criteria. So, let's start with targets of investigation.
There are two main types of information you
can look for that are relevant to AI moral
patienthood. The first is, is the system a moral
patient at all? And we call this welfare basis.
The second is, if it is a moral patient, what
is good or bad for it and how should we treat
it? And we call this welfare interests. If you're trying to establish welfare basis,
there are a few key things you can
look for that are widely considered candidates for
moral status. So probably the most intuitive is
consciousness. And by this, we mean some
kind of internal subjective experience, like there's something
it's like to be you. And a

another area is robust agency, and this is something like pursuing goals, having
desires and preferences. And here we use the
word "robust" to mean something different and probably
more demanding than the very broad way the
word "agent" is typically used in machine learning.
Audience: Is it definitely clear that desires and preferences go with just goals?
Presenter: I would not say any of this is

we define three different levels of agency, and
robust agency is kind of the most advanced,
which sort of incorporates many different features. So, yeah, goals as well as desires
and preferences. Whereas there are lower forms of
agency that are just about the goal idea.
So, I don't think they necessarily go hand
in hand, but this is kind of like
the cluster of things we're gesturing at when we talk about robust agency.
So, moving on to welfare interests. So, if you're trying to better understand
a system's welfare interests, you might be looking for things like,
if it was having experiences, would they likely be positive or negative experiences?
What are its preferences and are they currently
being satisfied or frustrated? And what are its
conditions for flourishing? What would it mean to
treat it well? Now, it's worth noticing that
you can study welfare basis and welfare interests
somewhat separately. So, here we have an example

some kind of genuine internal experience. But you
might think that if it was having
some kind of internal experience, it's probably not
having a very good time. So you might get
information about the welfare interests even if you
don't update much on the welfare basis.
Okay, so how can we get insight into welfare basis or welfare interests?
We're currently focused on three main types of
evidence. So behavioral evidence is what does it
say and do? Internal evidence is how does
it think, and developmental is how did it grow?
Okay, so starting off with behavioral evidence, there
are a couple of different types here. So
one is self-reports, which is what models say about themselves. Now, currently,
these are not very reliable. We don't have
strong reasons to believe that just because
a model says something, that that kind of
maps to some underlying internal state. But there
are proposals to improve reliability of self-reports. There's a paper that
Rob wrote with Ethan Perez that has some thoughts on this, and there are
some initial results from Jack Lindsey showing that self-reports can in fact accurately track
internal concepts. So it's possible, it's just a
question of when and how this is happening.
The second type of behavioral evidence is revealed
preferences. So this would be looking at what
models actually choose to do rather than just what they
say. And so, you might think that has fewer
inferential steps than self-reports because you're kind of
getting directly at what they are choosing
and not relying on the self-report being accurate.
And these, I think, can provide some evidence
about welfare interests even if they might be
dubious for updating you on welfare basis.
Behavioral evidence is great because you can easily run many experiments and scalably gather
evidence. It doesn't require access to the weights
or the activations or other internal features. So
you can do it on lots of different
types of models. You don't need that internal access.
But it suffers from a significant limitation, which
we call the mismatch problem. So when a
dog yelps and limps, we can reasonably infer
pain because we have a shared evolutionary heritage and
we have similar neural structures, but we can't
necessarily make the same inferences about AI.
And this is exacerbated by the fact that
AI is explicitly trained to produce convincing
outputs. So training can shape behaviors that superficially resemble welfare markers.
Right. So the second type is internal evidence. So
this is how does it think? Internal evidence aims
to look at the actual computations going on and the relevant affordances a model
has. So this could be architectural, looking at the type of the network,
the connectivity patterns, the scaffolding that's available.
So things like, does it have recurrent connections
that allow feedback processing? Does it have
long-term memory systems? And interpretability is another approach here. So looking actually at the
activations, the features, doing ablation studies where you're removing features or
components from a model to understand what actually contributes to its behavior. And so
here you might be asking questions like, does it have internal representations of
relevant concepts like pain? And do deception features activate when it's talking about its
own conscious experience? Internal evidence is cool because, unlike with biological systems,
we can record all the activations, we can
examine architectures in detail, and we can
intervene on specific computational processes. And it looks
under the hood, so we avoid this
mismatch problem that we had with behavioral evidence. But there are some limitations here.
We call this the specification problem — which computations actually matter.
If you go too general, then you could
end up in a situation where almost anything
qualifies. So if you think of a leading
theory of consciousness called global workspace theory,
and you're trying to look at whether a
model has something like a global workspace,
if you believe that anything with a central
information hub counts as a global workspace,
you could end up in a situation where
you're saying that networks of fewer than 10 neurons
would satisfy this consciousness criteria, which many people find intuitively implausible. On the
other hand, if you go too specific, then
you could end up missing genuine forms of
consciousness that just happen to be realized differently from how they work in humans.
Okay, moving on to developmental evidence. This aims
to think about the evolution of the system
and the kinds of pressures it's under. So,
one approach is reasoning from training objectives.
So, thinking about what sort of properties does
training tend to select for. For example, in RLHF,
people believe that this creates pressure to be sycophantic, and that could explain why
the model is highly suggestible when discussing sentience. Another approach here is to analyze
the developmental trajectory. So, looking at when and how different behaviors emerge. So,
for example, if a model is claiming it's
conscious, if those claims only emerge after
the helpfulness training, then maybe you could reason
it's more likely to be due to sycophancy.
And developmental reasoning is pretty common in general.
So, in AI safety, people often will ask
how likely powerful models are to be schemers.
And that tends to appeal to questions like, given
the training incentives of the model, how likely
are certain behaviors going to be selected for.
But this also has limitations. We call this the novel constraints problem. So
biological organisms share a common descent.

Okay, so moving on to research directions. So

Daniel Paleka looked into how consistent preferences are across different wording
